newsitem.title: THAILAND: Low steel, paper prices curb Siam Cement's profit.
newsitem.headline: Low steel, paper prices curb Siam Cement's profit.

text.p: Thailand's largest industrial conglomerate Siam Cement Plc said on Wednesday lacklustre performances by its steel and paper units because of poor prices led to a mere one percent rise in its second quarter profits.
It reported the group's consolidated profit of 1.7 billion baht in the second quarter compared with 1.68 billion baht in the same period last year.
"The dumping of imported steel made our steel business post losses in the quarter. The fall in world paper prices caused the paper units to post almost no profit," Chumpol told a news conference.
But analysts said the conglomerate's profit in the second quarter was above the expectations of most analysts' who had believed the group would post lower profits in the quarter.

"We expected Siam Cement's profit in the second quarter to be lower than the same period last year. Its second quarter results announced today were better than expected," Visit Ongpipattanakul, senior investment analyst at HSBC James Capel Asia Limited, told Reuters.

Siam Cement's share price closed 16 baht up on Wednesday at 944 baht and was the sixth most active trade. The share had plunged nearly 22 percent since July 5 on concern of its earnings in the second quarter.
Poor earnings by the group's steel and paper units caused its marginal earnings growth in the second quarter, Siam Cement president Chumpol Na Lamlieng told reporters.

But the traditional cement business which now contributes only about 30 percent of the group's total profit and building material units showed better earnings in the second quarter compared with the year-ago corresponding quarter, he said.
The group's earnings should pick up in the second half in anticipation of improving earnings from steel and paper businesses, Chumpol said.
"I believe that (steel and paper) prices have reached its lowest level," Chumpol said.
He expected the group's earnings from cement and building materials units to grow, albeit at a declining rate, due a slower trend in property construction.
"Our earnings from petrochemical, paper and auto parts business will grow substantially in the future due to rising consumption of these sectors," Chumpol said.
